summary: This informational RFC gives recommendations for how Internet Service Providers can handle malicious bot infestations on subscriber computers. Infected users risk data loss and fraud, and the machines can be used against others.

plainLanguage.summary: Some home computers get taken over by bad software. This tells internet providers how to notice and help their customers clean them up.

questions: how should isps handle infected customers
ways to notify users of malware
subtitle: How internet providers can detect and help users clean infected computers.

tldr.problem: Malicious bots installed on subscriber computers can send spam, participate in attacks, steal data, and turn machines into criminals tools. ISPs see traffic from these infected hosts but lack clear guidance on how to handle the situation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6561 provides recommendations for ISPs to detect bot-infected hosts, notify users through multiple channels, and offer remediation support (both self-service and professional assistance).
tldr.outcome: When ISPs actively detect and remediate bots, botnets shrink, spam and attacks decrease, and customers get help protecting their data and privacy.

facts.label: Bot definition
facts.value: Software installed without user consent, under remote control

facts.label: Primary infection vectors
facts.value: Unpatched systems, vulnerabilities, weak passwords, malicious sites

facts.label: Notification channels recommended
facts.value: Email, phone, walled garden, SMS, web browser, IM

facts.label: Most reliable remediation
facts.value: Complete OS reinstall from clean media with backup restore

today: RFC 6561 is an Internet Informational document published in March 2012 that reflects industry best practices for ISP response to botnet infections. ISPs continue to use these detection and notification methods, though malware has become more sophisticated. The remediation challenge remains a cat-and-mouse game, with new malware variants regularly circumventing existing detection and removal tools.

sections.title: What Are Bots and Why They Matter
sections.content:
A malicious bot is a program installed on a computer without the user's knowledge. It runs under remote control and performs tasks such as sending spam, stealing data, launching attacks, or hosting illegal content. A botnet is a network of such compromised machines, coordinated by criminals (bot masters) through command-and-control channels.

Bots infect machines through many routes: un-patched operating systems, software vulnerabilities, weak passwords, malicious websites, and social engineering. Because ISPs provide internet connectivity, they see traffic from infected machines leaving their networks. They are uniquely positioned to detect bots and notify users, who otherwise have no way of knowing their computer is compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: A bot is bad software that takes control of your computer without asking. Lots of infected computers are controlled by one criminal. Since your internet company sees all the traffic, they can often spot when one of your machines is infected.

sections.title: How ISPs Detect Bots
sections.content:
ISPs use multiple detection methods to identify infected hosts. These include:

Traffic analysis: Monitoring network flows for connections to known malware command-and-control servers or unusual patterns (like high volumes of outbound spam).

Data sharing: Receiving feeds from threat organizations and other ISPs listing IP addresses known to be infected or involved in attacks.

DNS analysis: Detecting queries to domain names known to be associated with malware.

Sinkholing and honeynets: Operating services that capture real-time data about bots attempting to join botnets.

Abuse complaints: Receiving reports from other ISPs, organizations, and victims about spam and attacks originating from the ISP's IP addresses.

ISPs should use multiple methods together to avoid false positives and confirm an actual infection before notifying users.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISP checks for: machines talking to known-bad servers, IP addresses on spam blacklists, weird patterns of activity, and complaints from other internet providers.

sections.title: Notifying Users About Infections
sections.content:
Once detected, the ISP should notify the user. The RFC recommends multiple notification methods, as each has limitations:

Email is common but messages may be filtered as spam or overlooked.

Phone calls are effective but costly.

Walled gardens restrict internet access until the user acknowledges the message and take action. Leaky walled gardens allow access to critical sites (patches, security vendors) while notification remains visible.

Web browser notifications display alerts when the user visits websites.

SMS and instant messaging provide direct contact but have cost and character limits.

The RFC recommends using multiple methods together. Notifications should be clear, avoid jargon, and include guidance on remediation. ISPs should allow users to register preferred contact methods, though not all should allow opting out entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISP tells the user their computer is infected. It can do this via email, a phone call, a warning pop-up, or by slowing the internet until they respond. Using several methods together works best.

sections.title: Helping Users Clean Their Machines
sections.content:
Remediation (removing the bot) can happen in two ways:

Guided self-remediation: The ISP provides a dedicated security website with clear, step-by-step instructions for non-technical users. Key steps include backing up personal files, installing operating system and antivirus updates, enabling automatic updates, and identifying which machine on the home network is infected. For knowledgeable users, more detailed technical guidance can be offered.

Professional assistance: Many users lack the technical skill to remove bots safely. ISPs should offer access to professional support, either online, by phone, or in-person. This may include partnerships with security forums or professional technicians.

ISPs should acknowledge that remediation is difficult. The most reliable way to ensure a bot is fully removed is to completely reinstall the operating system from clean media and restore files from a known-good backup. However, this is beyond the ability of most users.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISP gives the user a step-by-step guide: back up your files, update Windows, download a cleaner tool, run it. If that is too hard, the ISP can connect them with a technician to do it for them.

sections.title: Risks and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that remediation is not guaranteed to succeed. Sophisticated malware can hide in system memory, firmware, or secondary storage, making complete removal difficult or impossible without professional tools.

Notification itself carries risks. Attackers may spoof ISP notifications to trick users into installing more malware. ISPs must use authenticated notification methods and educate users on how to verify a genuine ISP message.

Some users will refuse to remediate. ISPs may track infection history and eventually terminate service for customers who repeatedly ignore remediation advice and continue hosting active botnets. However, this is a business decision, not a technical one.

Privacy is critical. ISPs should collect minimal personally identifiable information (PII) during bot detection and maintain it only as long as necessary. Data sharing with third parties (law enforcement, researchers) should be opt-in unless legally required.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys might send fake notifications to trick you. Some people will ignore the ISP and never clean their machines. The ISP must be careful not to collect too much personal information about infected users.
